newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Mexico, Caracas seen week's top Latam bolsa picks.
newsitem.headline: Mexico, Caracas seen week's top Latam bolsa picks.

text.p: Latin America's main bolsas were seen taking different cues this week as they emerge from Christmas and New Year celebrations, with Mexico and Venezuela likely to outperform the rest, dealers said.
Chile's bolsa was seen erratic while stocks in Brazil and Argentina were expected to put in a mixed performance.
In Mexico, traders predicted the stock market would wake from its recent slumber and aim for new record highs, piercing resistance at 3500 on the main IPC index, which it hit around midday.
The market was seen drawing strength from Wall Street and hopes of a local interest rate cut.
Despite the overall muted tone of the market last week, the IPC index rose 2.1 percent to 3396.95.
Analysts forecast the IPC would extend its rally, with volume swelling after a slow trading patch during the Christmas holiday season.
Stocks were also seen setting new record highs in Venezuela when financial markets reopen there Tuesday after the Epiphany holiday.
The market has been unexpectedly active during the holiday period thanks to expectations the economy will rebound sharply next year. "We expect this to continue," one trader said.

The Caracas bourse started 1996 with a bang, after last year scoring the biggest increases on the International Finance Corporation (IFC) index of emerging market equities with gains of nearly 115 percent.
Shares rose for the 11th consecutive session Friday, closing at a record 6.878,33 points.
In Chile investors remained focused on rumors of an impending Central Bank interest rate cut, which drove up the blue-chip .IPSA index nearly three percent on Friday.
But brokers saw no real underpinnings for the rally to continue unless rates come down or foreign demand strengthens.
"Predicting where the bolsa is going to go this week would be like playing the lottery," one dealer said.
Most brokers expected recovery to continue in electrical stocks, which took a beating in late 1996 on concerns about drought and competition on earnings.
The IPSA ended Friday at 103.22 points, up 3.2 percent since the index was readjusted to 100 on January 1.

Brazilian shares were seen mixed on moderate volume as investors await news on whether Brasilia will exempt stock trade from a new tax and any Congressional decision on a re-election bill, brokers said.
"It will be somewhat slow, with the market mostly following these two issues," one broker said.
The Sao Paulo bourse dipped 0.01 percent last week to close Friday at 69,978 points on thin trade.

The government is expected to decide this week if stocks will be exempt from the new 0.2 percent CPMF cheque tax, while Congress is likely to focus on debate on President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's bid to stand for re-election in 1998.
Players may also be nervous about December trade gap data due out next week. Some analysts have predicted it could reach a record $1.5 billion, taking the 1996 deficit to $5.2 billion.
Argentine stocks were also seen mixed, with many players holding their bets in a trading environment greatly conditioned by Wall Street.
"The pace will be dictated by the markets in New York," said analyst Guillermo Girard of Ro Valores.

Traders noted the bolsa had scant local incentives, although the undertone remained firm after recent gains thanks to steady economic recovery and expectations surrounding a rumored massive government bond placement in January.

"Wall Street has surged recently and I'm not optimistic for the short-run, because many key economic indicators are due out this week," said Girard. "But beyond this volatile patch, and especially if Friday's U.S. jobs report is stronger than expected and causes the markets to slump, I would see any correction as a buying opportunity."
The bolsa's blue-chip MerVal index .MERV jumped 2.0 percent last Friday to 651.83, recouping losses incurred in the previous two sessions to close narrowly higher for the week.
((-- Carmen Pignotti, Buenos Aires Newsroom 541 318-0657))
